item.text: {"question_id":"5B.4","answer":"In 2023, Sisi’s government adopted or directed several measures aimed at reducing business-formation and approval delays, facilitating land ownership and imports, expanding golden licenses, improving competitive neutrality, and supporting investment; it also ratified an amendment to the SME law (BATCH-0006-E020; BATCH-0006-E021; BATCH-0003-E006). These measures provide evidence of ruler-attributed formal policy action, but several were drafts, studies, assignments, or planned sales, and the supplied record does not verify consistent implementation or outcomes. Fairness and predictability remained materially constrained: the government prioritized military-owned enterprises, postponed opening military companies to private investors, and Sisi allocated new land to the army in early 2023; the record also describes privileged access for major investors and continuing marginalization of small farmers (BATCH-0009-R11-E001; BATCH-0009-R11-E009; BATCH-0009-R11-E010). Labor rules were likewise incompletely universal or enforceable: the private-sector minimum wage lacked binding enforcement and coverage excluded many private and informal workers, while female unemployment was reported at three times the male rate, although the latter finding is not specifically attributed to Sisi (BATCH-0021-E002; BATCH-0021-E004; BATCH-0005-E008). Recruitment-firm licensing and revocations show some sector-specific regulatory administration, but do not establish broad fair enforcement across the economy (BATCH-0009-R04-E003). The NTRA fine against Telecom Egypt is a discrete enforcement action, but the regulator’s subordination to the communications ministry limits what it demonstrates about independent competition regulation (BATCH-0002-E035). Overall, the evidence supports formal reform efforts alongside substantial implementation gaps, privileged state and investor access, weak labor enforcement, and unresolved limits on competition
